# The canonical register: Ahriman

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Ahriman, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Ahriman to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𐬀𐬢𐬭𐬀 𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬥𐬌𐬌𐬎**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Ahriman**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: say "ahriman" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Ahriman". The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *ahriman* differs from the canonical *Ahriman* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Medieval Zoroastrianism itself generated the most famous heresy about him: Zurvanism, attested in the Denkard's refutations and in Syriac and Armenian reports, made Ohrmazd and Ahriman twin sons of Zurvan, Infinite Time — evil suddenly genealogical rather than chosen, precisely the move orthodox theology refused.  Outside Iran, Plutarch (De Iside et Osiride 46–47) reports the Magi and their good and evil daimones, naming the evil one Arimanius; the name turns up again in a Greek magical papyrus (PGM IV), invoked there by sorcery.

And it never stopped working. Ahriman never had a cult — no sane theology worships the Lie — yet his legacy is immense.  In New Persian ahriman became an ordinary word for devil, and in Zoroastrian liturgy his name is ritually cursed to this day.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: Avestan scholarly transliteration as the liturgies are edited. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Ahriman** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Ahriman** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *ahriman* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Ahriman** stands at [/ahriman/](/ahriman/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 6 cited sources — Zarathustra, Gāthās: Yasna 30 (the two spirits) and 45 (the better and the bad), Vendidad 19 (the temptation of Zarathustra), Greater Bundahišn, trans. Agostini & Thrope, The Bundahišn (Oxford, 2020).
